# Introductions

## Git

The world’s most popular open source [version control system](../version-control-systems).

- **Distributed** - all developers maintain and share the code in their own local repositories, with no single central authority.

- **Repository versioning** - a new version number is issued for the repository as a whole, even when only one file has changed.

- Created by **Linus Torvalds** to help Linux kernel developers collaborate

## GitHub

A commercial web app used for hosting remote `git` repositories.

- Free hosting of repositories.

- Allows control over who can accesse each repository.

- Provides a web app and mobile apps for viewing repository files.

- Acquired by Microsoft for \$7.5 billion in 2018.

# Three-Tier Model

## Introduction

Git version control depends upon three tiers, or three places where files are stored.

- Working copy
- Staging index
- Repository

![Git tiers](../assets/version-control/git_tiers.png)

## Working copy

The copy of the files that a developer works on.

- Not tracked by git.

- Your ‘normal’ files you are already familiar with… almost.

![Working tree](../assets/version-control/git_working_tree.png)

## Staging index

A holding area for changes that *might* be included in the project’s official history.

- Allows developers pick and choose which changed files to include in the next commit to the repository

- [Read more](https://gitolite.com/uses-of-index.html) about some benefits of this

![Staging index](../assets/version-control/git_staging_index.png)

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge">

<div class="highlight">

``` highlight
# add any changed files within the working directory to the staging index
git add .
```

</div>

</div>

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge">

<div class="highlight">

``` highlight
# add only one file to the staging index
git add my_staging_index_slide.md
```

</div>

</div>

## Repository

The official history of the project, including the history of all committed files.

- With each commit, changed files in the staging index are moved to the repository

- A short one-line message describes the changes included in each commit

![Repository](../assets/version-control/git_repository.png)

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge">

<div class="highlight">

``` highlight
# commit any files in the staging index to the repository
git commit -m "Updating slide about git repositories"
```

</div>

</div>

# Git Terminology

## Introduction

A few terms we must familiarize ourselves with.

- Clone
- Fork
- Main
- Branch
- Remote
- Pull
- Push
- Merge
- Fetch
- Pull Request

## Clone

A new repository made by copying files from an existing repository.

- Typically involves creating a new local repository that is a copy of an existing remote repository.

- The new repository automatically keeps a link to the `origin` remote repository from which it came.

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge">

<div class="highlight">

``` highlight
# clone a remote repository onto the local machine
git clone https://github.com/your-github-handle/your-repository-name.git
```

</div>

</div>

![Clone](../assets/version-control/git_clone.png)

## Fork

Not a Git term, but rather a term used by remote repository hosting providers such as GitHub.

- A fancy word for creating a remote [clone](#clone) of a remote repository.

- A fork of a GitHub repository creates a clone of that repository in the active user’s own GitHub account

![Fork](../assets/version-control/git_fork.png)

## Main

The Git term for the `trunk` line of code.

- The default line of code that all commits are placed into unless other branch lines are created.

- PS: in earlier versions of `git`, the trunk was called `master`. You will still see this name used in many places.

![Main branch](../assets/version-control/git_main.png)

## Branch

The term for an offshoot of the `trunk` or `main` line of code.

- creating a branch allows developers to work on new code in isolation with no effect on the main `trunk` line.

- code in a branch can be `merged` into the trunk branch at any time, if desired

![Feature branch](../assets/version-control/git_branch.png)

When developers switch to a different branch, `git` **updates the working copy of the code** to match the state of the files in that branch.

The working copy, i.e. the codebase you see in your file system, always represents the code in the current branch.

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge">

<div class="highlight">

``` highlight
# see a list of all branches in the local repository
git branch
```

</div>

</div>

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge">

<div class="highlight">

``` highlight
# create a new branch
git branch experiment1
```

</div>

</div>

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge">

<div class="highlight">

``` highlight
# switch to the new branch
git checkout experiment1
```

</div>

</div>

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge">

<div class="highlight">

``` highlight
# switch back to the main branch
git checkout main
```

</div>

</div>

## Remote

A term used to mean a remote repository that the local repository is linked to.

- Typically, this refers to the remote repository from which a local repository was cloned.

- The nickname `origin` is usually used to refer to the original remote repository from which the local repository was cloned.

- The nickname `upstream` is also sometimes used to refer to a remote repository from which the `origin` repository was originally forked.

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge">

<div class="highlight">

``` highlight
# view a list of all currently known remotes
git remote -v
```

</div>

</div>

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge">

<div class="highlight">

``` highlight
# inform git of a remote and give it the nickname 'origin'
git remote add origin https://github.com/your-github-handle/your-repository-name.git
```

</div>

</div>

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge">

<div class="highlight">

``` highlight
# inform git of a remote and give it the nickname 'upstream'
git remote add upstream https://github.com/some-other-github-handle/some-other-repository-name.git
```

</div>

</div>

## Pull

Download and merge any changes *in the current branch* from a remote repository to the local repository.

- It’s good practice to `pull` before you `push`.

![Pull](../assets/version-control/git_pull.png)

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge">

<div class="highlight">

``` highlight
# download and merge any changes in the main branch from the 'origin' remote repository to the local repository
git pull origin main
```

</div>

</div>

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge">

<div class="highlight">

``` highlight
# download and merge any changes in the main branch from the 'upstream' remote repository to the local repository
git pull upstream main
```

</div>

</div>

## Push

Upload changes from the local repository to a remote repository.

![Push](../assets/version-control/git_push.png)

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge">

<div class="highlight">

``` highlight
# Upload any changs in the main branch from the local repository to the 'origin' remote repository
git push origin main
```

</div>

</div>

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge">

<div class="highlight">

``` highlight
# Upload any changs in the main branch from the local repository to the 'upstream' remote repository
git push upstream main
```

</div>

</div>

## Fetch

Download but do not automatically merge any changes *in the current branch* from a remote repository to the local repository.

- This is similar to `git pull`, but `pull` automatically merges any changes into the current branch, while `fetch` does not.

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge">

<div class="highlight">

``` highlight
# fetch any changes from the remote repository
git fetch origin
```

</div>

</div>

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge">

<div class="highlight">

``` highlight
# fetch any changes from the 'upstream' remote repository
git fetch upstream
```

</div>

</div>

## Merge

Take the changes from one branch or repository and incorporate them into another branch or repository.

- If both branches include recent changes to the same lines of code, `git` will inform you of a conflict.

- Any such merge conflicts must be manually resolved using your preferred editor.

![Merge](../assets/version-control/git_merge.png)

- A typical workflow:

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge">

<div class="highlight">

``` highlight
git pull origin main # get latest code for the current branch from the remote origin repository

git checkout some-branch-name # switch to a branch where you will make changes in isolation... either first create this branch with `git branch some-branch-name` or do `git checkout -b some-branch-name` to create it and check it out at once

# make some chages to the code in this branch, if desired using your preferred editor
# stage and commit your changes, i.e. `git add .`, `git commit -m "some message."`

git checkout main # switch back to the main branch to prepare to merge

git pull origin main # download any recent changes from the origin server

git merge some-branch-name # incorporaate your changes in the branch into the code in the main branch

git branch -d some-branch-name # delete the branch now that we're done with it

git push origin main # upload your changes to the remote origin repository
```

</div>

</div>

## Pull Request

A request to another GitHub user to approve changes you have made and to merge those changes from one branch or repository into another.

- A **pull request** is a GitHub feature, not a `git` feature.
- One user requests another user to review the code and approve its merger.
- The reviewer can **approve** or **reject** the request outright, or add comments that ask the initiator of the pull request to make changes to the code before the pull request can be approved.

## Pull Request (continued)

The purpose of a Pull Request is to enforce a **peer review** of the code before it is merged into the main branch.

- All team members must share the responsibility of reviewing each-others’ code.

\-

- No team member should *ever* approve their own pull request.

\-

To generate a [CSV](/content/courses/database-design/slides/plain-text-data-formats#comma-separated-values-csv) file showing the latest `50` pull requests for a given repository, run the following command using [GitHub’s Command-Line Interface](https://cli.github.com/):

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge">

<div class="highlight">

``` highlight
gh pr list --state merged --json number,createdAt,title,author,mergedBy --template '{{range .}}{{.number}},{{.createdAt}},{{"\""}}{{.title}}{{"\""}},opened by {{.author.login}},merged by {{.mergedBy.login}}{{"\n"}}{{end}}' -L 50 -R https://github.com/team-repository-url
```

</div>

</div>

## Pull Request (continued)

As pull requests are a GitHub feature, not a `git` feature, they are not included in `git` [logs](#logs). To view a list of pull requests…

- view them in your GitHub repository’s `Pull Requests` tab.

- install the [GitHub Command-Line Interface](https://cli.github.com/) and use the [`gh pr list`](https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_pr_list) command.

- a version that shows more metadata, including who created and approved each pull request, where `<your_github_repository_url>` is replaced with the relevant URL of your GitHub repository:

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge">

<div class="highlight">

``` highlight
gh pr list --state merged --json number,createdAt,title,author,mergedBy --template '{{range .}}{{.number}},{{.createdAt}},{{"\""}}{{.title}}{{"\""}},opened by {{.author.login}},merged by {{.mergedBy.login}}{{"\n"}}{{end}}' -L 50 -R <your_github_repository_url>
```

</div>

</div>

This last command can be useful to check whether any developer has approved his or her own pull requests, which is forbidden!

# Creating a Local Repository

## Introduction

A local repository can be created in one of two ways:

1.  from scratch
2.  as a clone of an existing repository

## From scratch

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge">

<div class="highlight">

``` highlight
mkdir project0
cd project0
git init
```

</div>

</div>

If you later decide to link a local repository to a remote repository:

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge">

<div class="highlight">

``` highlight
git remote add origin git@github.com:YOUR-USERNAME/YOUR-REPOSITORY.git
```

</div>

</div>

## As a clone of an existing repository

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge">

<div class="highlight">

``` highlight
git clone https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/YOUR-REPOSITORY.git
```

</div>

</div>

# Tracking Changes with the Local Repository

## Introduction

Changes in the Working Copy (adding, modifying, or deleting files) are not tracked.

Files must be added to the staging index in order to be tracked.

## Add files to the staging index

Make any changes you desire.

Then add all the modified files in working copy to the staging index:

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge">

<div class="highlight">

``` highlight
git add .
```

</div>

</div>

# Committing Changes to the Local Repository

## Introduction

The staging index does not maintain the history of all changes.

Changes must be moved to the repository in order to be fully archived.

Commit all changes in the staging index to the repository:

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge">

<div class="highlight">

``` highlight
git commit -m 'resolving issue #23'
```

</div>

</div>

# Sharing Changes with Other Developers

## Introduction

Any changes to the local repository must usually be shared with other developers.

For this reason, they should frequently be uploaded to a shared remote repository.

## Pushing changes to the remote repository

Push the code in the current branch from the local repository to the branch named ‘main’ on the remote repository called ‘origin’:

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge">

<div class="highlight">

``` highlight
git pull
git push origin main
```

</div>

</div>

Optionally, you can set `origin` as the default place to push by running this command once:

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge">

<div class="highlight">

``` highlight
git push --set-upstream origin main
```

</div>

</div>

From then on, you can use just `git push` to push changes to `origin`.

# Merge Conflicts

## Introduction

Conflicts may occur in a number of scenarios:

- When **pulling** code from a remote repository to a local repository.
- When **pushing** code from a local repository to a remote repository.
- When **merging** code from one **branch** into another.
- When **merging** code from one **repository** into another.

Git will merge code automatically, if possible, and ask the developer to do it themselves, if not.

# Configuration

## Introduction

Several important configurations that **must be completed** prior to versioning:

- configure `git` username and email address to match that of GitHub
- remove any GitHub “`Name`” field settings
- turn off rebasing
- always leave single-line commit messages
- use `.gitignore` to exclude files from versioning

## Git username and email address

Local git `user.name` and `user.email` settings must match **exactly** your login name and email set up on GitHub:

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge">

<div class="highlight">

``` highlight
git config --global user.name "monalisa"
```

</div>

</div>

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge">

<div class="highlight">

``` highlight
git config --global user.email "mona.lisa@mlouvre.org"
```

</div>

</div>

**Note**: If you *must* use a different email or username configuration for this course than for other work you do with `git`, you can change `--global` to `--local` in the above commands to make these configurations for one specific repository. However, *the burden would then be on you* to ensure you repeat this configuration for each repository in this course or risk not having your work counted.

## GitHub name

Leave blank the `Name` field in your GitHub account settings to be sure that your username is used instead for all commits. *This is not optional*.

![GitHub username settings](../assets/git-github/github-username-settings.png)

If you *must* use a specific `Name` configuration in GitHub for another course or job that requires it, you should **create a separate GitHub account for this course** with no `Name` value.

## Turn off rebasing

`git` has two ways it can handle `pull` events, where changes from a remote repository are downloaded and integrated into the local repository: `merge` and [rebase](https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2/Git-Branching-Rebasing). We want to use `merge` because this maintains the full history of the project, whereas `rebase` changes the history to make it simpler and you thus may not receive credit for your full contribution to a project.

To turn off rebasing and use regular merging, you **must** run this command:

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge">

<div class="highlight">

``` highlight
git config --global pull.rebase false
```

</div>

</div>

Read more about [rebase vs. merge](https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2/Git-Branching-Rebasing) if interested - note the last section of the document.

## Enforce single-line commit messages

Multi-line commit messages are considered invalid bad code, according to our development conventions.

- **Commit messages must be one line**: concise yet descriptive enough to give a sense of what has changed.

- It is possible to enforce the one-line commit message rule by creating a [git commit-msg hook](https://git-scm.com/docs/githooks#_commit_msg) - a script that runs with every commit to check that the commit message has been formatted according to the chosen conventions.

- A [git commit-msg hook that enforces single-line commit messages](https://gist.github.com/bloombar/b202ecbdab6b542a52761f316c7a5c4d) has been created for you to use in all of your repositories. Simply save the given file named `commit-msg` into a `.githooks` subdirectory of a repository’s main directory, make it executable with `chmod a+x .githooks/commit-msg`, and then run `git config core.hooksPath .githooks` to enable it for the given repository.

- Once implemented, the hook will auto-reject any attempts to commit with multi-line messages to the repository, ensuring the team is following its commit message conventions. This must be reconfigured for every new repository.

## .gitignore

A file in the project directory named `.gitignore` instructs Git to ignore certain files or directories.

This *absolutely must* include instructions to ignore any platform code and 3rd party modules.

View an [example](https://gist.github.com/bloombar/1bbca4aafb267920ac220864d99d6c8f)

# Logs

## Introduction

Git maintains a log of all commits to the repository. To see this:

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge">

<div class="highlight">

``` highlight
git log
```

</div>

</div>

Hit the `SPACE` bar to scroll through the logs and hit `q` to quit when you’re done.

## Options

There are a few useful options when viewing logs.

- show a list of all commits in a compact format

  <div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge">

  <div class="highlight">

  ``` highlight
  git log --oneline
  ```

  </div>

  </div>

- show all commits with a few statistics of what was changed in each

  <div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge">

  <div class="highlight">

  ``` highlight
  git log --shortstat
  ```

  </div>

  </div>

… and many more

## gitlogstats

A Famous developer has created the [gitlogstats](https://pypi.org/project/gitlogstats/) tool to generate a summary of the logs, with many additional options.

e.g., find all contributions to a repository over a specific time period:

<div class="language-bash highlighter-rouge">

<div class="highlight">

``` highlight
gitlogstats -s 11/15/2024 -e 12/15/2024 -r https://github.com/some-repo.git
```

</div>

</div>
